title: The Rising Tide of Kidney Disease in Nigeria: Causes, Warning Signs, and Prevention Strategies
text:
Dr. Sotomiwa Sotubo, a nephrologist at LASUTH and LASUCOM, discusses the major causes and warning signs of kidney disease in Nigeria, and provides crucial insights into protecting kidney health and preventing kidney failure.
Kidney disease, a silent but significant health issue, is on the rise in Nigeria, with approximately one in ten Nigeria ns estimated to be affected. Dr. Sotomiwa Sotubo, a consultant nephrologist at the Lagos State University Teaching Hospital (LASUTH) and lecturer at the Lagos State University College of Medicine (LASUCOM), discusses the major causes, warning signs, and prevention strategies for this potentially life-threatening condition in an interview with NKECHI ONYEDIKA-UGOEZE.
The kidneys, two bean-shaped organs located below the rib cage, play a crucial role in filtering blood, removing waste products, maintaining fluid balance, and producing vital hormones like erythropoietin and calcitriol. Kidney failure, if left unaddressed, can lead to severe complications such as anemia, bone diseases, and even death. Currently, Nigeria's inadequate healthcare infrastructure and high treatment costs make accessing dialysis challenging, highlighting the importance of prevention and early detection.
The primary risk factors for kidney disease in Nigeria are hypertension and diabetes, followed by chronic glomerulonephritis. Other factors include obesity, prostate problems, recurrent urinary tract infections, kidney stones, family history, certain medications, excessive alcohol consumption, and smoking. Regular medical checks, blood pressure monitoring, and proper management of underlying conditions can significantly reduce the risk of kidney failure.
Dr. Sotubo has treated patients as young as 13 and 18 on dialysis, emphasizing the need for routine kidney screening from adulthood, with increased frequency after the age of 40 and for those with a family history of kidney disease
